<reason>PRO kept the motion framed as the correct counterfactual (same city, same demand, more legal supply) and made CON carry the heavy burden of showing that two decades of durable added stock would be fully offset. PRO's "busts are cyclical, bans are permanent" asymmetry and the point that Seattle/Denver being pricier than their own pasts measures demand, not supply's effect, were never squarely answered—CON's "exactly, demand swamps supply" move misdescribes PRO's point as a concession. PRO also handled the crash pressure adequately (2004–07 units still stand; 2011+ recovery strangled by zoning; Phoenix/Vegas were speculative sprawl, not infill into near-zero vacancy). CON fought well and landed real hits: the "denser, not sprawl" reading undercut Houston/Phoenix as exhibits, the price-to-income yardstick inconsistency was fair, and the option-value answer to PRO's Q1 was coherent. But CON's countervailing mechanisms (land uplift, induced migration, demolition) are second-order relative to the stock argument, its "name a metro" test demands an experiment PRO correctly noted was never run, and its Rebuttal 1 was clipped. Clear but competitive win for PRO.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 2 pivot—"read the motion: it says denser housing; Houston and Phoenix are sprawl stories smuggled in as density evidence"—was the sharpest single hit, damaging PRO's exhibits; PRO's closing answered with the counterfactual/direction framing and "the 2009 vacancy is gone, the 2009 building still shelters someone," which preserved PRO's core route even without those exhibits.</best_rebuttal>
